How alike do the two images of each hard pair look to a vision model, as the stimuli move from photo toward abstraction
(photo → cut-out → illustration → line drawing → doodle)? Embeddings come from `pipeline/12_embeddings.py`:
DINOv3 ViT-B/16 (LVD-1689M, pooled CLS) and CLIP ViT-B/32 (the model used in CHS). Similarity is cosine between the
pair's two images. Formats that have not been generated yet are simply absent.

```{python}
#| include: false
import sys, warnings; warnings.filterwarnings('ignore'); sys.path.insert(0, '../pipeline')
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from config import OUT, pairs, words
P, W = pairs(), words()
ORDER = ['CHS photo', 'photo', 'cutout', 'illustration', 'illustration_cutout', 'line', 'line_cutout', 'doodle', 'doodle_cutout']
FINAL = ORDER[1:]                      # the new stimuli (all 16 pairs); CHS photo has the 13 CHS pairs only
MODELS = {'dinov3': 'DINOv3 ViT-B/16', 'clip': 'CLIP ViT-B/32'}
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)

def load(model):
    z = np.load(f'{OUT}/embeddings_{model}.npz')
    return {tuple(k.split('|')): e for k, e in zip(z['key'], z['emb'])}
E = {m: load(m) for m in MODELS}

def pair_table(Em):
    """Per version x pair: raw pair similarity, the same-format baseline (mean similarity of A and of B to every other
    image in that format), the excess over it, and the partner's rank among the other images (1 = more similar than all)."""
    rows = []
    for v in sorted({v for v, _ in Em}):
        ws = [w for w in W if (v, w) in Em]; ix = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(ws)}
        X = np.stack([Em[(v, w)] for w in ws]); S = X @ X.T
        for r in P.itertuples():
            if r.word_a not in ix or r.word_b not in ix: continue
            a, b = ix[r.word_a], ix[r.word_b]; o = [i for i in range(len(ws)) if i not in (a, b)]
            base = (S[a, o].mean() + S[b, o].mean()) / 2
            rows.append(dict(version=v, pair=r.pair, domain=r.domain, sim=S[a, b], baseline=base, excess=S[a, b] - base,
                             rank=np.mean(np.r_[S[a, b] > S[a, o], S[a, b] > S[b, o]])))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
T = {m: pair_table(E[m]) for m in MODELS}
fmts = [f for f in ORDER if f in set(T['dinov3'].version)]
```

## Raw similarity rises with abstraction, but so does everything else

```{python}
for m, name in MODELS.items():
    d = T[m][T[m].version.isin(fmts)]
    print(name); print(d.groupby('version')[['sim', 'baseline', 'excess', 'rank']].mean().reindex(fmts).round(3).to_string(), '\n')
```

Raw pair similarity goes up as detail is removed. The same-format baseline goes up as much or more: once photo
texture, lighting and scene are gone, *any* two images in a style resemble each other. Raw cosine is therefore not
comparable across formats. On an LWL trial the target and distractor are always shown in the same format, so the
model quantity that matters is the pair's similarity *relative to its format*: the excess, or the partner's rank.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, (m, name) in zip(axes, MODELS.items()):
    g = T[m].groupby('version')[['sim', 'baseline', 'excess']].agg(['mean', 'sem']).reindex(fmts)
    for col, c in [('sim', 'k'), ('baseline', 'tab:grey'), ('excess', 'tab:red')]:
        ax.errorbar(range(len(fmts)), g[(col, 'mean')].values, yerr=1.96 * g[(col, 'sem')].values, marker='o', color=c, capsize=3,
                    label={'sim': 'pair similarity', 'baseline': 'same-format baseline', 'excess': 'pair − baseline'}[col])
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(fmts))); ax.set_xticklabels(fmts, rotation=25, ha='right'); ax.set_title(name); ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=.3)
axes[0].set_ylabel('cosine'); axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9); fig.tight_layout()
```

## Per pair: which pairs does abstraction separate, and which does it merge?

Excess similarity per pair. If abstraction removed exactly the details that make a pair confusable, the pair's
excess should fall; if it removed the details that tell the two apart, it should rise.

```{python}
for m, name in MODELS.items():
    w = T[m].pivot(index='pair', columns='version', values='excess')[[f for f in FINAL if f in fmts]]
    print(name); print(w.sort_values('photo').round(3).to_string(), '\n')
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
fin = [f for f in FINAL if f in fmts]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=True)
for ax, (m, name) in zip(axes, MODELS.items()):
    w = T[m].pivot(index='pair', columns='version', values='excess')[fin]
    for i, (p, row) in enumerate(w.iterrows()):
        c = plt.cm.tab20(i % 20); ax.plot(range(len(fin)), row.values, marker='o', ms=4, color=c, lw=1.2)
        ax.text(len(fin) - 1 + .08, row.values[-1], p, fontsize=7, color=c, va='center')
    ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=.6); ax.set_xticks(range(len(fin))); ax.set_xticklabels(fin, rotation=25, ha='right')
    ax.set_xlim(-.3, len(fin) + .8); ax.set_title(name); ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=.3)
axes[0].set_ylabel('pair similarity − same-format baseline'); fig.tight_layout()
```

How much of the item ordering survives each format change? Spearman correlation of per-pair excess across the 16 pairs:

```{python}
for m, name in MODELS.items():
    w = T[m].pivot(index='pair', columns='version', values='excess')[fin]
    print(name); print(w.corr(method='spearman').round(2).to_string(), '\n')
```

## A recognition-side model measure: CLIP word → image 2AFC

Embedding similarity is not recognition. Closer to the task: give CLIP the spoken word ("a photo of a {word}" /
"a drawing of a {word}") and ask whether it prefers the target over its partner, in each format. In CHS photos CLIP was
at ceiling, so this mainly shows whether any format pulls it off ceiling.

```{python}
import torch, open_clip
clip, _, _ = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms('ViT-B-32', pretrained='openai'); clip.eval(); tok = open_clip.get_tokenizer('ViT-B-32')
TEMPL = ['a photo of a {}.', 'a drawing of a {}.', 'an illustration of a {}.', 'a picture of a {}.']
label = lambda w: 'chicken' if w.startswith('chicken') else w
with torch.no_grad():
    TX = {}
    for w in W:
        t = clip.encode_text(tok([s.format(label(w)) for s in TEMPL])); t = t / t.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        t = t.mean(0); TX[w] = (t / t.norm()).numpy()
partner = {**dict(zip(P.word_a, P.word_b)), **dict(zip(P.word_b, P.word_a))}
rows = []
for v in fmts:
    for w in W:
        if (v, w) not in E['clip'] or (v, partner[w]) not in E['clip']: continue
        lo = 100 * np.array([E['clip'][(v, w)] @ TX[w], E['clip'][(v, w)] @ TX[partner[w]]])
        rows.append(dict(version=v, word=w, p_correct=np.exp(lo[0]) / np.exp(lo).sum()))
rec = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(rec.groupby('version').p_correct.agg(['mean', 'min', lambda s: (s < .5).sum()]).rename(columns={'<lambda_0>': 'n wrong'}).reindex(fmts).round(3).to_string())
```

```{python}
print(rec.pivot(index='word', columns='version', values='p_correct')[fmts].round(2).sort_values('photo').head(12).to_string())
```

## Illustration rounds

Words whose illustration was regenerated (round 0 = first pass; final = current `stimuli/images/illustration`).
Only pairs containing a regenerated word can change.

```{python}
for m, name in MODELS.items():
    d = T[m]; rr = sorted(v for v in d.version.unique() if 'round' in v)
    if not rr: continue
    cols = [v for v in rr if v.startswith('illustration round')] + ['illustration'] + \
           [v for v in rr if v.startswith('illustration_cutout round')] + ['illustration_cutout']
    w = d.pivot(index='pair', columns='version', values='excess')[cols]
    print(name); print(w[(w.max(axis=1) - w.min(axis=1)) > 1e-4].round(3).to_string(), '\n')
```

## What this means for the format hypothesis

- **Raw similarity rises steadily with abstraction** (DINOv3 .13 photo → .34 doodle; CLIP .71 → .82–.83), but almost all
  of the rise is the same-format baseline: in a sparse style every image looks like every other.
- **Relative to its format, the pair-specific similarity barely moves, and the two models disagree on direction.**
  DINOv3 excess goes .10 (photo) → .13 (illustration) → .10–.17 (line, doodle); CLIP goes .10 → .08 → .05–.07.
- **Model recognition does fall for the most abstract formats.** CLIP word → image 2AFC is at ceiling for photos,
  cut-outs and illustrations (≥ .99) but drops for line drawings and doodles (.89–.93 mean, with individual words
  near or below chance). Some of that is stimulus quality (the acorn doodle looks like garlic; the snake line drawing
  is buried in background scribble), so the per-word failures should be re-checked after the redos.
- **That gives a clean prediction to set against children.** The models say abstraction leaves pairs about as
  separable (embeddings) or makes the words harder to recognise (CLIP 2AFC). If toddlers instead recognise words as
  well or better in illustrations and line drawings, the details removed by abstraction (texture, lighting,
  background) were noise for them rather than cues: a model–child dissociation.
- **The item-level test is sharper.** Some pairs' excess moves in opposite directions across formats (lizard–snake
  drops, acorn–coconut and cow–horse rise). A format × model-score interaction on baseline-corrected looking tests
  whether item-specific model changes predict children's item-specific changes; a format main effect with a null
  interaction is the dissociation.
- **Caveats.** Cosine on a pooled embedding is one readout of a model. Illustrations differ from photos in colour as
  well as detail, so line drawings and doodles are the cleaner "fewer details" contrast, but they are also the
  noisiest stimuli right now (see `04_stylized_stimuli`). With 16 pairs the item-level interaction has little power;
  the format main effect is the realistic primary test.
